cards.body:
Dawn Miller, 49, was admitted to Cleveland Clinic Martin North Hospital in Port St. Lucie on February 24, 2024, with abdominal pain. She underwent emergency surgery the following day to remove her gallbladder. Two days later, pathology confirmed she had gangrenous cholecystitis, a severe and life-threatening gallbladder condition. Medical records show that on February 27, a hospital employee sent a formal query asking Dawn's doctor to confirm whether she had severe sepsis, a life-threatening response to infection in which the body starts damaging its own tissues. About an hour and 15 minutes later, the response checked the box next to severe sepsis with acute lactic acidosis, present on admission.

Dawn was discharged on the morning of February 28, 2024, at 9:16 a.m. Her mother, Beth Miller, says within minutes of getting home, her daughter collapsed. Beth performed CPR while waiting for emergency services. Emergency records show Dawn was back at Cleveland Clinic Martin North by 10:40 that morning with no pulse. Staff immediately began chest compressions, but at 11:11 a.m., she was pronounced dead. Beth requested an autopsy, and two nurses documented that request before Dawn was sent to the morgue. However, a nurse manager later wrote that the medical examiner released the body and was not requiring an autopsy.

Dr. Gerald Feigin, a forensic pathologist who reviewed Dawn's medical records, said her chemistries were not normal. Bloodwork taken five hours before her discharge showed at least eight components flagged as either high or low, and a basic metabolic panel indicated low kidney function. Feigin was most concerned about the drop in Dawn's hemoglobin to 8.2, which the Cleveland Clinic's own website states is a severe low level. When asked directly whether Dawn should ever have been discharged, Feigin said absolutely not. Cleveland Clinic was contacted for comment but declined to answer questions, citing patient privacy laws. Records from the Florida Department of Health show no public complaints or disciplinary actions against any of the doctors involved. Additional records from the Agency for Health Care Administration show no disciplinary action against the hospital.

Peter Solomon Ruma, 37, of Vero Beach was arrested Wednesday on eight charges stemming from the creation and distribution of AI-generated sexually explicit images of women without their consent. The charges relate to incidents occurring between June and August 2026 involving one female victim, according to the Vero Beach Police Department.

Ruma faces three counts of creation of an altered sexual depiction of an identifiable person, three counts of promotion of an altered sexual depiction of an identifiable person, one count of sexual cyberharassment, and one count of stalking. Detectives executed search warrants on Ruma's residence and electronic devices during the investigation. A forensic examination recovered evidence investigators believe is associated with the creation and distribution of altered sexual images. Photographs obtained from social media and other online sources were used to create some of the altered images, according to police.

During the course of the investigation, detectives identified several additional females believed to have been victimized through similar conduct. Investigators also have information indicating Ruma may have engaged in this type of conduct for several years. Detectives believe there may be additional victims who have not yet been identified or who may be unaware that altered sexual images depicting them were created or distributed. Court records show Ruma has a prior criminal history in Indian River County. In 2007, he was arrested on charges that included burglary and sex battery on a physically impaired person. In 2009, he was arrested on a burglary charge and was later sentenced to the Florida Department of Corrections.

Ruma is currently being held at the Indian River County Sheriff's Office on a $1 million bond. The investigation remains ongoing, and additional charges may be forthcoming as additional victims or evidence are identified. The Vero Beach Police Department thanked the victim for coming forward, saying her cooperation was instrumental in the investigation. The Indian River County Sheriff's Office and the State Attorney's Office also assisted throughout the investigation. Anyone who believes they may have been victimized by Ruma, or who has received, viewed, or has information regarding altered or sexually explicit images allegedly created or distributed by Ruma, is encouraged to contact Detective Matakaetis of the Vero Beach Police Department at (772) 978-4665. Those wishing to remain anonymous can contact Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers at 800-273-8477 and may be eligible for a cash reward.

Investigators have identified several additional potential victims who have not been identified or may not know images of them were created or shared. hero.body:
Martin County authorities confirmed that a body found in the mangroves near the House of Refuge on Hutchinson Island is that of Michael Anthony Debevec, who was reported missing last week after visiting Chastain Beach. Investigators with the Martin County Sheriff's Office found Debevec's body Tuesday after an extensive search of the area. Detectives reported they have not found any apparent signs of foul play. The Medical Examiner has not yet determined Debevec's cause of death.

 The search began after a Good Samaritan found a wallet Saturday belonging to Debevec and went to Debevec's home in an attempt to return it, prompting his family to report him missing. Investigators later found Debevec's vehicle at Chastain Beach, more than two miles from where his body was ultimately discovered.

 Sheriff John Budensiek said investigators determined Debevec traveled from the Port St. Lucie area to Martin County at about 3 a.m. August 27 and parked at Chastain Beach. Phone records showed Debevec's phone was in use Friday morning and moving between Chastain Beach and the House of Refuge, according to investigators.

 On Tuesday morning, investigators found a backpack belonging to Debevec hanging high in a tree with his computer inside. A deeper search into the mangroves led investigators to the body. The Martin County Sheriff's Office thanked the community members who shared information about Debevec and helped with the search. Debevec's family has been notified of his death.

hero.body:
St. Lucie County commissioners voted Tuesday to remove automated license plate readers, including Flock cameras, from county-owned roads and property, while also halting the issuance of new permits and potentially revoking existing ones. The vote follows earlier restrictions imposed by the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office limiting license plate reader use to forcible felony investigations and missing person cases.

 The motion, introduced by Commissioner James Clasby, passed 3-2. Commissioner Erin Lowry said during the meeting, "I feel like everywhere you turn now in our community is a Flock camera." Clasby emphasized the need to protect residents' privacy, saying, "And I believe that we need to protect our citizens and order the removal from our right-of-way. It's actually mind-boggling. It's almost impossible to go anywhere without being tagged by at least one."

 Commissioner Cathy Townsend and another member voted against the measure, expressing a desire for input from local law enforcement before making a decision. Commissioner Jamie Fowler questioned the handling of data collected by the cameras during the discussion. In July, Paris Lewbel, a spokesperson for Flock Safety, explained that data collected by the cameras is controlled by the agency using them and is deleted after 30 days by default. Every search within the Flock platform is recorded in an immutable audit log, which tracks who conducted the search, the reason, and the parameters.

 St. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro released a statement saying his office would comply with the state order to remove cameras from state highways and tighten internal rules but did not call for their removal from county roads. Port St. Lucie Police Chief John Bolduc also announced an operational pause on automated license plate readers. The decision by the county commissioners goes beyond the Florida Department of Transportation's directive to remove cameras from state highways, extending the removal to county-controlled public rights of way.

St. Lucie County commissioners voted 3-2 Tuesday to remove automated license plate readers, including Flock cameras, from county-owned roads and property, halt the issuance of new permits and potentially revoke existing ones. The decision goes beyond the Florida Department of Transportation's directive to remove cameras from state highways, extending the removal to county-controlled public rights of way. Commissioner James Clasby introduced the motion, saying he believes the county needs to protect citizens and order the removal from the right-of-way. Commissioner Erin Lowry said the cameras have become a nuisance, adding that it feels like everywhere you turn in the community is a Flock camera.

Commissioner Cathy Townsend and another member voted against the motion, with Townsend expressing a desire to let the three heads of law enforcement in the county educate commissioners more before making a decision. Commissioner Jamie Fowler questioned the handling of data collected by the cameras and whether it is being used properly. Clasby said it is almost impossible to go anywhere without being tagged by at least one camera.

St. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro released a statement saying his office would comply with the state order to remove cameras from state highways and tighten internal rules but did not call for their removal from county roads. Port St. Lucie Police Chief John Bolduc announced an operational pause on automated license plate readers. The Sheriff's Office is imposing new restrictions on the use of automated license plate reader technology, limiting its use to forcible felony investigations and missing-person cases.

Paris Lewbel, a spokesperson for Flock Safety, said in July that data collected by the cameras is controlled by the agency using them and is deleted after 30 days by default. Lewbel said every search within the Flock platform is recorded in an immutable audit log, which tracks who conducted the search, the reason and the parameters. The county has not yet resolved how existing permits will be handled or how quickly cameras will come down.

Chavi Rose-Marie Hammock was arrested August 28 on an active warrant charging her with grand theft and uttering a forged instrument. The Indian River County Sheriff's Office said the case originated after law enforcement in New York reported that two checks had allegedly been altered and deposited into a TD Bank account belonging to Hammock. One of the checks was changed from $800 to $17,658 before it was deposited, according to investigators.

Detectives said bank records showed deposits totaling $37,316 were made into Hammock's account in October 2024. Investigators allege that cash withdrawals followed, including a withdrawal of $16,500, before the account was later closed. Surveillance images and video provided by TD Bank appeared to show Hammock conducting transactions connected to the deposits and withdrawals, according to the warrant affidavit. A witness later identified Hammock from surveillance photos.

Authorities allege the transactions occurred between October and November 2024 and resulted in more than $37,000 being obtained through fraudulent means. Hammock was booked into the Indian River County Jail and faces charges of grand theft and uttering a forged instrument. The case remains under investigation.

A 37-year-old Vero Beach man was arrested Wednesday on eight charges after investigators say he used artificial intelligence to create and distribute sexually explicit images of women without their consent. Peter Solomon Ruma faces three counts of creation of an altered sexual depiction of an identifiable person, three counts of promotion of an altered sexual depiction of an identifiable person, one count of sexual cyberharassment, and one count of stalking. He is being held at the Indian River County Sheriff's Office on a $1 million bond.

Detectives with the Vero Beach Police Department executed search warrants on Ruma's residence and electronic devices during the investigation. A forensic examination of those devices resulted in the recovery of evidence investigators believe is associated with the creation and distribution of altered sexual images. Photographs obtained from social media and other online sources were used to create some of the altered images, according to police.

The current charges stem from incidents occurring between June and August 2026 and relate to one female victim. During the course of the investigation, detectives identified several additional females believed to have been victimized through similar conduct. Investigators also have information indicating Ruma may have engaged in this type of conduct for several years. Court records show Ruma has a prior criminal history in Indian River County, with a 2007 arrest on charges that included burglary and sex battery on a physically impaired person, and a 2009 burglary charge that resulted in a sentence to the Florida Department of Corrections.

Detectives believe there may be additional victims who have not yet been identified or who may be unaware that altered sexual images depicting them were created or distributed. Anyone who believes they may have been victimized by Ruma, or who has received, viewed, or has information regarding altered or sexually explicit images allegedly created or distributed by Ruma, is encouraged to contact Detective Matakaetis of the Vero Beach Police Department at (772) 978-4665. Those wishing to remain anonymous can contact Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers at 800-273-8477 and may be eligible for a cash reward. The investigation remains ongoing, and additional charges may be forthcoming as additional victims or evidence are identified.
